desc:
Encoding. A singly linked list is passed to your function as an array holding the node values from head to tail; an empty array is an empty list. You may build real nodes from it first, or work on the array directly. Lists you return are given as arrays of values from head to tail.

The list a is sorted in non-decreasing order, but the list b is sorted in non-increasing order (largest value first). Merge them into a single list sorted in non-decreasing order and return its values from head to tail.

For a = [1,4,6] and b = [7,5,5,2] the answer is [1,2,4,5,5,6,7]. The textbook merge of two ascending lists does not apply directly: the nodes of b have to be consumed from the other end. Try to do it in O(n + m) time with O(1) extra space by relinking nodes.
constraints: a is non-decreasing, b is non-increasing
hints: Sorting everything would work but ignores the structure. What is special about the order of b?
The smallest value of b is its tail, which a singly linked list cannot reach quickly. What operation turns a non-increasing list into a non-decreasing one?
Reverse b in place (a single pass), then run the standard two-pointer merge of two non-decreasing lists with a dummy head and a tail pointer.
editorial: First reverse b by flipping its next pointers; this takes O(m) time and O(1) space and makes it non-decreasing. Then merge as usual: compare the two heads, append the smaller to the tail of the result, and advance in that list. When one list is exhausted, link the remainder of the other list.

Total time is O(n + m) and extra space is O(1). A different but equivalent idea is to build the answer from the large end: the largest remaining value is either the tail of a or the head of b, and prepending nodes to the result avoids reversing anything, but it needs the tail of a and so a reversal of a instead.
